denomProfiles.tagline: Filipino nationalist church of catholic order, in full communion with Anglicans and Old Catholics.
coreDoctrines: The 1947 Declaration of Faith and Articles of Religion affirm the Trinity, the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds and the authority of Scripture.
Holds the historic episcopate, received from bishops of the US Episcopal Church in 1948, as essential to its catholic order.
Seven sacraments are retained, with baptism and the Eucharist treated as pre-eminent.
Teaches that the Church must be self-governing and rooted in Filipino culture rather than ruled by foreign clergy.
Understands the gospel as calling the Church to work for justice, human rights and the poor.
focuses: Filipino national identity and independence from foreign ecclesiastical control.
Social justice, labour rights and advocacy for peasants and indigenous peoples.
Ecumenical partnership with the Episcopal Church in the Philippines and the wider Anglican Communion.
Pastoral care of overseas Filipino workers and diaspora parishes.
practices: Celebrates a catholic-style Mass, now largely in Filipino and other Philippine languages.
Clergy may marry; the church ordains women to the priesthood, a practice begun in the late 1990s.
Led by an elected Obispo Máximo (Supreme Bishop) and a synod-based episcopate.
Trains many of its clergy at St Andrew's Theological Seminary in Quezon City, shared with Philippine Episcopalians.
Honours the memory of Filipino patriots and clergy martyrs, such as the priests Gómez, Burgos and Zamora executed in 1872.

influencedBy.name: Roman Catholic Church
influencedBy.text: It inherited the Spanish Catholic liturgy, sacramental system and parish structure of the islands.

influencedBy.name: Philippine Revolution
influencedBy.text: The anti-Spanish revolution of 1896–98 and the Filipino clergy movement shaped its nationalist programme.

influencedBy.name: Episcopal Church (United States)
influencedBy.text: Episcopal bishops consecrated its bishops in 1948 and a concordat of full communion followed in 1961.

influencedBy.name: Old Catholic Churches
influencedBy.text: The 1965 agreement with the Union of Utrecht brought full communion and shared catholic-but-not-papal ecclesiology.

influenced.name: Episcopal Church in the Philippines
influenced.text: The two churches share a seminary, joint ministries and a long-standing concordat of full communion.

influenced.name: Philippine ecumenical social activism
influenced.text: Its bishops and clergy have been prominent in the National Council of Churches in the Philippines and human-rights campaigns.

keyFigures.name: Isabelo de los Reyes
keyFigures.role: Labour leader and journalist who proclaimed the church in 1902.

keyFigures.name: Gregorio Aglipay
keyFigures.role: Former Catholic priest and revolutionary chaplain; first Obispo Máximo (1902–40).

keyFigures.name: Isabelo de los Reyes Jr
keyFigures.role: Obispo Máximo who led the return to Trinitarian orthodoxy and the 1948 consecrations.

keyFigures.name: Alberto Ramento
keyFigures.role: Former Obispo Máximo and human-rights advocate, murdered in Tarlac in 2006.

denomProfiles.tagline: Communion of self-governing churches keeping the faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
coreDoctrines: Accepts the seven Ecumenical Councils (Nicaea 325 to Nicaea II 787) and the Nicene–Constantinopolitan Creed without the Filioque.
Holy Tradition, of which Scripture (with the Septuagint Old Testament) is the heart, is the rule of faith, interpreted by the Fathers and councils.
Salvation is theosis: participation in God's uncreated energies, while God's essence remains unknowable (Gregory Palamas, councils of 1341–51).
The veneration of icons is upheld as a confession of the Incarnation, celebrated on the Sunday of Orthodoxy (843).
The Church is a conciliar communion of local churches; the Ecumenical Patriarch holds a primacy of honour, not universal jurisdiction.
Mary is honoured as Theotokos and ever-virgin; the saints and the departed are commemorated in prayer.
focuses: The Divine Liturgy as the centre of church life and the experience of heaven on earth.
Monasticism, above all Mount Athos, as the spiritual heart of the Church.
Hesychast prayer and the Jesus Prayer, collected in the Philokalia (1782).
Continuity with the Church Fathers and resistance to doctrinal innovation.
Ecclesial unity across nations, despite recurring jurisdictional disputes.
practices: Celebrates the Liturgies of St John Chrysostom and St Basil in Greek, Church Slavonic, Arabic, Romanian and many vernaculars.
Baptises infants by triple immersion and immediately chrismates them and gives them Communion.
Keeps four fasting seasons and Wednesday and Friday fasts; Pascha is the feast of feasts.
Churches have an iconostasis; worshippers venerate icons, light candles and often stand.
Parish priests may marry before ordination; bishops are drawn from celibate monastics.
Some churches follow the Julian calendar, others the Revised Julian for fixed feasts, while all keep Pascha on the Julian reckoning (except Finland).

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: Orthodoxy sees itself as the unbroken continuation of the apostolic and patristic Church.

influencedBy.name: Cappadocian Fathers
influencedBy.text: Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa gave Orthodox Trinitarian theology its classic form.

influencedBy.name: Byzantine Empire
influencedBy.text: Imperial Constantinople shaped its liturgy, canon law, church architecture and idea of church–state symphonia.

influencedBy.name: Desert Fathers
influencedBy.text: Egyptian and Syrian monasticism formed its ascetic and spiritual tradition.

influenced.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influenced.text: The conversion of Kyivan Rus in 988 carried Byzantine Orthodoxy to the Slavic north.

influenced.name: Eastern Catholic Churches
influenced.text: Byzantine-rite Catholic churches keep Orthodox liturgy and spirituality in communion with Rome.

influenced.name: Slavonic letters
influenced.text: The mission of Cyril and Methodius created Slavonic literacy and the basis of the Cyrillic alphabet.

influenced.name: Western ressourcement and ecumenism
influenced.text: Émigré theologians such as Lossky and Florovsky influenced 20th-century Western theology and the World Council of Churches.

keyFigures.name: John Chrysostom
keyFigures.role: Archbishop of Constantinople whose liturgy is the Church's usual Eucharistic rite.

keyFigures.name: John of Damascus
keyFigures.role: Systematiser of Orthodox doctrine and defender of icons.

keyFigures.name: Photius I
keyFigures.role: Patriarch of Constantinople and critic of the Filioque in the 9th century.

keyFigures.name: Gregory Palamas
keyFigures.role: Defender of hesychasm and the essence–energies distinction.

keyFigures.name: Maximus the Confessor
keyFigures.role: Theologian of the two wills of Christ and of deification.

members.note: Pew Research Center (2017) estimate of Orthodox Christians worldwide; this total also includes Oriental Orthodox churches such as the Ethiopian.

denomProfiles.inIndia: Eastern Orthodoxy is very small in India; a few Indian communities are under the Ecumenical Patriarchate's Metropolis of Singapore and South Asia (created 2008). India's 'Orthodox' Christians in Kerala belong mainly to the Oriental Orthodox family instead.

denomProfiles.tagline: Largest Orthodox church, heir of the 988 baptism of Rus and of Moscow's patriarchate.
coreDoctrines: Shares the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils and the Creed without the Filioque.
Sees itself as the canonical church of the lands of historic Rus, including Russia, Belarus and (in its view) Ukraine.
Holds a strong theology of holy tradition, the saints and the New Martyrs of the Soviet era, canonised in large numbers in 2000.
Its 2000 'Bases of the Social Concept' sets out teaching on church–state relations, family, bioethics and war.
Emphasises church–state 'symphony' and a civilisational vision, recently expressed as the 'Russian world' (Russkii mir).
focuses: Rebuilding parishes, monasteries and seminaries after Soviet persecution; tens of thousands of churches reopened after 1988.
Monastic and elder (starets) spirituality, from Sergius of Radonezh to the Optina elders.
Preserving Church Slavonic worship and the Julian calendar.
A public role in Russian national life, which critics, including many Orthodox theologians, regard as too close to state power.
practices: Long services in Church Slavonic, including the all-night vigil, with congregations usually standing.
Keeps the Julian calendar, celebrating Christmas on 7 January (civil calendar).
Rich traditions of icon painting (Andrei Rublev's Trinity) and bell-ringing.
Strict fasting before Communion and in the Great Fast; frequent confession before receiving.
Mass pilgrimages to relics and monasteries such as the Trinity–St Sergius Lavra.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Rus received its faith, liturgy and first metropolitans from Constantinople.

influencedBy.name: Bulgarian Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Church Slavonic books and clergy came to Rus largely through Bulgaria.

influencedBy.name: Paisius Velichkovsky and the Philokalia
influencedBy.text: His Slavonic Dobrotolubie (1793) sparked the 19th-century revival of eldership.

influencedBy.name: Petrine Synodal system
influencedBy.text: Peter the Great's abolition of the patriarchate (1721) placed the church under a state Holy Synod until 1917.

influenced.name: Old Believers
influenced.text: Opponents of Patriarch Nikon's reforms broke away after the councils of 1666–67.

influenced.name: Orthodox Church in America
influenced.text: Grew from the Russian mission to Alaska (1794) and received autocephaly from Moscow in 1970.

influenced.name: Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia
influenced.text: Émigré bishops organised abroad after the revolution and reunited with Moscow in 2007.

influenced.name: Russian religious philosophy
influenced.text: Thinkers such as Khomyakov, Soloviev and Bulgakov drew on and reshaped Russian Orthodox thought.

keyFigures.name: Vladimir the Great
keyFigures.role: Prince of Kyiv whose baptism in 988 began the Christianisation of Rus.

keyFigures.name: Sergius of Radonezh
keyFigures.role: 14th-century monastic founder and Russia's best-loved saint.

keyFigures.name: Patriarch Nikon
keyFigures.role: Reformer of the 1650s whose liturgical changes provoked the Old Believer schism.

keyFigures.name: Tikhon of Moscow
keyFigures.role: First patriarch after the restoration of 1917 and confessor under Soviet rule.

keyFigures.name: Patriarch Kirill
keyFigures.role: Patriarch since 2009, associated with the church's revival and with the 'Russian world' doctrine.

members.note: Pew Research Center (2017) figure for Orthodox Christians in Russia, most of whom identify with the Moscow Patriarchate; the Patriarchate's own claims, which include Belarus, Ukraine and the diaspora, are much higher.

denomProfiles.tagline: Historic see of New Rome, first in honour among Orthodox churches.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Claims, on the basis of canon 3 of Constantinople (381) and canon 28 of Chalcedon (451), a primacy of honour among Orthodox churches.
Teaches that it may hear appeals and grant autocephaly; this role is contested, especially by Moscow.
Asserts jurisdiction over the Orthodox diaspora outside the territories of other autocephalous churches.
Has championed the theological case for environmental care as a spiritual responsibility.
focuses: Pan-Orthodox coordination, culminating in the Holy and Great Council in Crete (2016).
Ecumenical dialogue, notably with Rome since Athenagoras and Paul VI lifted the 1054 anathemas in 1965.
Survival of a tiny Greek Orthodox community in Turkey and the reopening of the Halki seminary, closed in 1971.
Pastoral care of Greek-speaking and other diaspora churches in America, Britain and Australia.
Creation care, earning Patriarch Bartholomew the nickname 'Green Patriarch'.
practices: The Patriarch resides at the Phanar in Istanbul, with the Patriarchal Church of St George.
Celebrates the Byzantine liturgy in its classical Greek form and Byzantine chant.
Follows the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts, adopted in 1923–24.
Oversees Mount Athos, the semi-autonomous Church of Crete, the Dodecanese and the autonomous churches of Finland and Estonia.
Turkish law requires the Patriarch to be a Turkish citizen, narrowing the pool of candidates.

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: Constantinople inherited the faith of the councils, several of which it hosted.

influencedBy.name: Byzantine Empire
influencedBy.text: Its prestige derived from being the see of the imperial capital, 'New Rome'.

influencedBy.name: Ottoman millet system
influencedBy.text: After 1453 the Patriarch became civil head (ethnarch) of all Orthodox subjects of the Sultan.

influenced.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influenced.text: Constantinople sent the first metropolitans of Kyiv and recognised the Moscow patriarchate in 1589.

influenced.name: Church of Greece
influenced.text: Granted autocephaly to the Greek church by Tomos in 1850.

influenced.name: Orthodox Church of Ukraine
influenced.text: Granted it a Tomos of autocephaly in January 2019.

influenced.name: Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
influenced.text: The Kyivan metropolitanate that entered the Union of Brest (1596) had been under Constantinople.

keyFigures.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
keyFigures.role: Archbishop of Constantinople who presided briefly over the Council of 381.

keyFigures.name: Photius I
keyFigures.role: Patriarch at the centre of the 9th-century dispute with Rome.

keyFigures.name: Cyril Lucaris
keyFigures.role: 17th-century patriarch whose Calvinist-leaning Confession (1629) caused controversy.

keyFigures.name: Athenagoras I
keyFigures.role: Patriarch (1948–72) who met Pope Paul VI in Jerusalem in 1964.

keyFigures.name: Bartholomew I
keyFigures.role: Patriarch since 1991, active in ecumenism, environmentalism and the Ukrainian question.

denomProfiles.tagline: The autocephalous Orthodox church of most of Greece, the nation's 'prevailing religion'.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith; doctrine is set by the Ecumenical Councils and Holy Tradition.
The Greek constitution (Article 3) names the Eastern Orthodox Church of Christ the 'prevailing religion' and binds it dogmatically to Constantinople.
Its Charter requires the Holy Synod to preserve unity of faith with the Ecumenical Patriarchate and the other Orthodox churches.
Treats the Greek-language New Testament and the Septuagint as the Church's authoritative biblical text.
focuses: Close bonds between Orthodoxy and Greek national identity since the War of Independence (1821).
Lay renewal movements such as Zoe (1907) and Apostoliki Diakonia, the church's mission and publishing arm.
A theological revival from the 1960s, associated with thinkers such as Christos Yannaras.
Social welfare through parishes, especially during the economic crisis after 2010.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Koine Greek with Byzantine chant; name days are widely celebrated.
Adopted the Revised Julian calendar in 1924, prompting the Old Calendarist schism.
Holy Week and Pascha are national festivals, with the midnight 'Christos anesti' and candlelit processions.
Governed by the Archbishop of Athens and All Greece with the Holy Synod; clergy salaries have long been paid by the state.
Crete and the Dodecanese stay under Constantinople, and the northern 'New Lands' are administered by Athens on Constantinople's behalf (1928 Act).

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Its mother church, which recognised its autocephaly in 1850.

influencedBy.name: Bavarian regency of King Otto
influencedBy.text: Unilateral autocephaly in 1833 was shaped by the regency's state-church model, influenced by Georg von Maurer.

influencedBy.name: Kollyvades movement
influencedBy.text: Athonite monks such as Nikodemos the Hagiorite promoted frequent Communion and published the Philokalia (1782).

influenced.name: Greek Old Calendarists
influenced.text: Churches of the Genuine Orthodox Christians separated in protest at the 1924 calendar change.

influenced.name: Orthodox Autocephalous Church of Albania
influenced.text: Greek-trained clergy and the Greek missiologist Anastasios played a key role in its revival.

influenced.name: Orthodox mission in Africa
influenced.text: Greek theologians and missionary societies supported the African dioceses of the Patriarchate of Alexandria.

keyFigures.name: Nikodemos the Hagiorite
keyFigures.role: Editor of the Philokalia and the Pedalion (Rudder) of canon law.

keyFigures.name: Chrysostomos (Papadopoulos)
keyFigures.role: Archbishop of Athens who introduced the Revised Julian calendar in 1924.

keyFigures.name: Christodoulos
keyFigures.role: Archbishop (1998–2008) known for his public, national profile.

keyFigures.name: Ieronymos II
keyFigures.role: Archbishop of Athens and All Greece since 2008.

denomProfiles.tagline: Arabic-speaking Orthodox patriarchate of the city where disciples were first called Christians.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith and the Chalcedonian Christology accepted at the Council of 451.
Claims succession from the apostle Peter and from Ignatius of Antioch at the see of Antioch.
Stresses a conciliar Orthodoxy open to its Arab cultural setting and to dialogue with Muslims.
Recognises the canonical territory of other Orthodox churches, and has defended its own in disputes, such as with Jerusalem over Qatar.
focuses: Witness of Arab Christians in Syria and Lebanon amid war, emigration and kidnapping of clergy.
Youth and lay renewal through the Orthodox Youth Movement, founded in Lebanon in 1942.
Education, notably the University of Balamand in Lebanon (1988).
A large diaspora in the Americas and Australia, open to Western converts.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Arabic, with Greek and, in the diaspora, English.
The Patriarch has resided in Damascus since the 14th century.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
Its North American archdiocese received Evangelical Orthodox converts in 1987 and allows a Western Rite vicariate.

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: Antioch was one of the earliest Christian centres (Acts 11:26) and a leading patriarchate of the ancient Church.

influencedBy.name: Antiochene school
influencedBy.text: Its literal, historical style of exegesis shaped preachers such as John Chrysostom.

influencedBy.name: Arab Christian nationalism
influencedBy.text: The election of the Arab Patriarch Meletios Doumani in 1899 ended Greek control of the hierarchy.

influenced.name: Melkite Greek Catholic Church
influenced.text: A pro-Catholic party separated in 1724 to form a Byzantine-rite church in communion with Rome.

influenced.name: Evangelical converts in America
influenced.text: Peter Gillquist's Evangelical Orthodox Church entered its North American archdiocese in 1987.

keyFigures.name: Ignatius of Antioch
keyFigures.role: Early-2nd-century bishop and martyr, revered as a founding father of the see.

keyFigures.name: John Chrysostom
keyFigures.role: Antiochene priest and preacher before becoming Archbishop of Constantinople.

keyFigures.name: Georges Khodr
keyFigures.role: Metropolitan of Mount Lebanon and co-founder of the Orthodox Youth Movement.

keyFigures.name: Ignatius IV (Hazim)
keyFigures.role: Patriarch (1979–2012) and founder of the University of Balamand.

keyFigures.name: John X (Yazigi)
keyFigures.role: Patriarch since 2012.

denomProfiles.tagline: Greek Orthodox patriarchate of St Mark, now chiefly a missionary church across Africa.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith, including the Chalcedonian definition rejected by the Coptic majority of Egypt.
Claims succession from the evangelist Mark and from Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria.
Claims jurisdiction over the whole of Africa, a claim tested since 2021 by Moscow's rival African exarchate.
In 2016 its synod decided to restore the female diaconate, an ancient order, consecrating deaconesses in the Congo in 2017.
focuses: Missionary growth in sub-Saharan Africa: Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, the Congo, Nigeria and beyond.
Translation of the liturgy into African languages and training of African clergy.
Care for the remnant Greek communities of Egypt.
Schools, clinics and orphanages run through its African dioceses.
practices: The Patriarch resides in Alexandria and bears the title Pope and Patriarch.
Byzantine liturgy in Greek, Arabic, English, French, Swahili, Luganda and other languages.
African dioceses grew from the 1920s movement of Reuben Spartas Mukasa in Uganda, received by Alexandria in 1946.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: Alexandria was the great theological centre of the early Church.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: After 451 the Chalcedonian minority looked to Constantinople, and Byzantine rites replaced the Alexandrian.

influencedBy.name: African Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Reuben Spartas and Obadiah Basajjakitalo first found Orthodoxy via Alexander McGuire's African Orthodox Church.

influenced.name: African Orthodoxy
influenced.text: Its mission created Orthodox churches with African clergy and bishops in more than a dozen countries.

influenced.name: Orthodox Church of Ukraine
influenced.text: Its 2019 recognition of the OCU led Moscow to break communion and set up its own exarchate in Africa.

keyFigures.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
keyFigures.role: 4th-century bishop and champion of Nicaea, revered by both Alexandrian patriarchates.

keyFigures.name: Cyril of Alexandria
keyFigures.role: 5th-century patriarch and theologian of the Council of Ephesus.

keyFigures.name: Reuben Spartas Mukasa
keyFigures.role: Ugandan founder of the Orthodox movement in East Africa.

keyFigures.name: Theodoros II
keyFigures.role: Pope and Patriarch since 2004, who has emphasised African mission.

denomProfiles.tagline: Mother Church of Jerusalem, guardian of the Holy Sepulchre and the holy places.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Claims descent from the first Christian community led by James, the brother of the Lord.
Raised to a patriarchate at the Council of Chalcedon (451) under Bishop Juvenal.
Sees itself as custodian of the holy places on behalf of the whole Orthodox world.
focuses: Guardianship of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Church of the Nativity, shared under the Ottoman 'Status Quo'.
Pastoral care of Arabic-speaking Orthodox Christians in Israel, Palestine and Jordan.
Hospitality to pilgrims from across the Orthodox world.
Management of extensive church lands, a source of controversy over sales and leases.
practices: Its hierarchy is drawn from the Greek-speaking monastic Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre, while most laity are Arab.
The ceremony of the Holy Fire on Holy Saturday at the tomb of Christ draws vast crowds.
Keeps the Julian calendar.
The Patriarch consecrates the Archbishop of the autonomous Church of Mount Sinai (St Catherine's Monastery).

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: The Jerusalem church of Acts is the earliest Christian community.

influencedBy.name: Byzantine imperial patronage
influencedBy.text: Constantine's Holy Sepulchre and later Byzantine building made Jerusalem a pilgrimage centre.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: From Ottoman times its patriarchs were largely Greek and closely tied to Constantinople.

influenced.name: Arab Orthodox movement
influenced.text: Arab laity have campaigned since the late 19th century for a greater role in the patriarchate.

influenced.name: Pilgrimage piety
influenced.text: Liturgies of Jerusalem shaped the Church's year, including Holy Week and the stational liturgy described by Egeria.

keyFigures.name: James, brother of the Lord
keyFigures.role: Leader of the Jerusalem church, venerated as its first bishop.

keyFigures.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: 4th-century bishop whose catechetical lectures describe the Jerusalem rites.

keyFigures.name: Sophronius
keyFigures.role: Patriarch who surrendered Jerusalem to the Caliph Umar in 638.

keyFigures.name: Theophilos III
keyFigures.role: Patriarch since 2005, after the deposition of Irenaios I.

denomProfiles.tagline: Church of St Sava, bound up with Serbian identity and the monasteries of Kosovo.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
'Svetosavlje', the spiritual legacy of St Sava, presents Orthodoxy and Serbian identity as deeply intertwined.
Venerates the 'Kosovo covenant', the choice of the heavenly over the earthly kingdom linked to the Battle of Kosovo (1389).
Teaching shaped by 20th-century theologians Justin Popović and Nikolaj Velimirović, both canonised.
focuses: Preservation of medieval monasteries in Kosovo, such as Peć, Visoki Dečani and Gračanica (UNESCO sites).
Serbian communities across the former Yugoslavia, Montenegro and the diaspora.
Monastic revival after communism.
Remembrance of 20th-century suffering, including the Jasenovac camp in the Second World War.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic, increasingly also in Serbian.
Keeps the Julian calendar; Christmas on 7 January with the badnjak (Yule log).
The krsna slava, a family feast of its patron saint, is a distinctive household tradition.
Led by the Patriarch of Serbia, with his seat in Belgrade and the historic see at Peć.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Granted Sava autocephaly in 1219 from its exile seat at Nicaea.

influencedBy.name: Mount Athos
influencedBy.text: Sava was a monk of Athos and founded the Serbian monastery of Hilandar there with his father.

influencedBy.name: Cyril and Methodius mission
influencedBy.text: Slavonic liturgy and letters reached Serbia from the Byzantine–Bulgarian missions.

influenced.name: Macedonian Orthodox Church
influenced.text: The Ohrid Archbishopric, which declared autocephaly from Belgrade in 1967, was granted it by Serbia in 2022.

influenced.name: Orthodox in Montenegro and Bosnia
influenced.text: Its dioceses shape church life in Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia.

keyFigures.name: Sava
keyFigures.role: First Archbishop of the autocephalous Serbian church (1219) and its patron saint.

keyFigures.name: Stefan Dušan
keyFigures.role: Tsar who raised the archbishopric to a patriarchate in 1346.

keyFigures.name: Justin Popović
keyFigures.role: Theologian and monastic, canonised in 2010.

keyFigures.name: Patriarch Pavle
keyFigures.role: Ascetic patriarch (1990–2009) through the Yugoslav wars.

keyFigures.name: Patriarch Porfirije
keyFigures.role: Patriarch since 2021.

denomProfiles.tagline: Orthodoxy of a Latin people: the second-largest Orthodox church in the world.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Its theology was renewed by Dumitru Stăniloae, whose Romanian Philokalia and Dogmatic Theology are classics.
Sees Orthodoxy as integral to Romanian identity while affirming religious freedom under the 1990s democratic order.
Emphasises a 'philokalic' tradition of prayer descending from Paisius Velichkovsky's revival at Neamț.
focuses: Rebuilding church life after communism, including thousands of new churches and the People's Salvation Cathedral in Bucharest (consecrated 2018).
Monastic life, with many monasteries in Moldavia and Bukovina.
Diaspora parishes for millions of Romanian emigrants in Western Europe.
Religious education in state schools and social work.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Romanian, in use since the 17th–18th centuries (Bucharest Bible, 1688).
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts (since 1924).
The painted monasteries of Bukovina, with exterior frescoes, are UNESCO World Heritage sites.
Led by a Patriarch (since 1925) and a Holy Synod; Patriarch Daniel has served since 2007.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Recognised the church's autocephaly in 1885.

influencedBy.name: Paisius Velichkovsky
influencedBy.text: His monastic school at Neamț in the 18th century spread hesychast prayer across the Slavic and Romanian lands.

influencedBy.name: Bulgarian and Serbian Slavonic tradition
influencedBy.text: Church Slavonic was the liturgical language of the Romanian lands until the vernacular replaced it.

influenced.name: Romanian Greek Catholic Church
influenced.text: Created by the 1700 union at Alba Iulia; forcibly absorbed into the Orthodox church in 1948 and restored in 1989–90.

influenced.name: Global Orthodox theology
influenced.text: Stăniloae's work on the Trinity and deification shaped Orthodox and ecumenical theology.

keyFigures.name: Paisius Velichkovsky
keyFigures.role: 18th-century abbot of Neamț and reviver of hesychast prayer.

keyFigures.name: Miron Cristea
keyFigures.role: First Patriarch of Romania (1925–39).

keyFigures.name: Justinian Marina
keyFigures.role: Patriarch (1948–77) who steered the church under communist rule.

keyFigures.name: Dumitru Stăniloae
keyFigures.role: The leading Romanian Orthodox theologian of the 20th century.

keyFigures.name: Patriarch Daniel
keyFigures.role: Patriarch since 2007.

members.note: Approximate number of people declaring Orthodox religion in Romania's 2021 census, roughly three-quarters of the population; excludes Moldova and the diaspora.

denomProfiles.tagline: First Slavic national church, cradle of Slavonic letters and the Cyrillic script.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Treasures the legacy of Cyril and Methodius and their disciples as the foundation of Slavonic Christianity.
Was declared schismatic by Constantinople in 1872 for 'phyletism' (organising the church by ethnicity); the schism ended in 1945.
Left the World Council of Churches in 1998, reflecting conservative suspicion of ecumenism.
focuses: Preserving Orthodoxy as part of Bulgarian national identity, especially after Ottoman and communist rule.
Monastic heritage, above all Rila Monastery, founded by John of Rila.
Restoring church life and unity after the 1992–2012 schism with an alternative synod.
Rebuilding parish life, religious education and monasteries after the communist period (1944–89).
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic and Bulgarian.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts (since 1968).
Led by a Patriarch of Bulgaria and Metropolitan of Sofia; Daniil was elected in 2024.
Popular feasts such as St George's Day and the Epiphany diving for the cross in rivers.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Bulgaria received Byzantine Christianity under Khan Boris I in 864–65.

influencedBy.name: Cyril and Methodius mission
influencedBy.text: Their disciples Clement and Naum, expelled from Moravia, built Slavonic schools at Ohrid and Preslav.

influencedBy.name: Bulgarian national revival
influencedBy.text: The 19th-century revival campaigned for the Bulgarian Exarchate, created by Ottoman firman in 1870.

influenced.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influenced.text: Slavonic books and clergy from Bulgaria helped form the church of Kyivan Rus.

influenced.name: Serbian Orthodox Church
influenced.text: The Ohrid literary school shaped Slavonic church life in Serbia and Macedonia.

influenced.name: Slavonic literacy
influenced.text: The Preslav and Ohrid schools spread the Cyrillic and Glagolitic scripts across the Slavic world.

keyFigures.name: Boris I
keyFigures.role: Ruler who converted Bulgaria to Christianity in the 860s.

keyFigures.name: Cyril and Methodius
keyFigures.role: Byzantine missionaries whose disciples brought Slavonic letters to Bulgaria.

keyFigures.name: Clement of Ohrid
keyFigures.role: Disciple of Methodius, bishop and teacher of thousands of Slavonic clergy.

keyFigures.name: John of Rila
keyFigures.role: 10th-century hermit and Bulgaria's patron saint.

keyFigures.name: Euthymius of Tarnovo
keyFigures.role: 14th-century patriarch, hesychast and reformer of Slavonic texts.

denomProfiles.tagline: Ancient church of St Nino and one of Georgia's most trusted institutions.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Treasures its conversion through St Nino in the 330s and its tradition of apostolic preaching by Andrew.
Its autocephaly, dating from Antiochene grants in the early medieval period, was abolished by Russia in 1811, restored in 1917 and recognised by Constantinople in 1990.
Sees Orthodoxy as inseparable from Georgian language, culture and statehood.
focuses: National and cultural identity, especially since independence in 1991.
Monastic revival and church building after the Soviet era.
Family and demographic concerns, such as the Patriarch's mass baptisms of third and later children since 2008.
Conservative moral teaching in public debates.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Georgian, with distinctive polyphonic chant.
Keeps the Julian calendar.
Led by the Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia, a title used since the 11th century; Ilia II was enthroned in 1977.
The grapevine cross of St Nino is the church's emblem; Svetitskhoveli Cathedral in Mtskheta is its mother church.

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: Georgia received Christianity under King Mirian III through St Nino.

influencedBy.name: Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch
influencedBy.text: Georgia's church was originally linked to Antioch, which recognised its autonomy.

influencedBy.name: Russian Empire
influencedBy.text: Annexation led to Russian control of the church (1811–1917) and Russification of church life.

influenced.name: Monasticism abroad
influenced.text: Georgian monks founded Iviron on Mount Athos and the Monastery of the Cross in Jerusalem.

influenced.name: Georgian literature
influenced.text: Georgian script and literature developed largely through Bible translation and hagiography.

keyFigures.name: Nino of Georgia
keyFigures.role: Woman evangelist who converted the royal house in the 4th century.

keyFigures.name: Mirian III
keyFigures.role: King of Iberia, first Christian ruler of Georgia.

keyFigures.name: David IV the Builder
keyFigures.role: 12th-century king who founded Gelati Monastery and reformed the church.

keyFigures.name: Ilia II
keyFigures.role: Catholicos-Patriarch enthroned in 1977, central to the church's post-Soviet revival.

members.note: About 83% of Georgia's population declared Orthodox in the 2014 census of the National Statistics Office of Georgia.

denomProfiles.tagline: Apostolic church of Barnabas, autocephalous since the Council of Ephesus.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Traces its foundation to the apostles Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13).
Its independence from Antioch was confirmed by canon 8 of the Council of Ephesus (431).
Emperor Zeno confirmed its autocephaly in 488 after Barnabas's relics were reportedly found.
focuses: Leadership of the Greek Cypriot community, inherited from the Ottoman role of the Archbishop as ethnarch.
Care for churches and monasteries in the north, inaccessible or damaged since the Turkish invasion of 1974.
Monastic centres such as Kykkos Monastery.
Education and charitable work, supported by substantial church property.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Greek.
The Archbishop keeps imperial privileges granted by Zeno: signing in red ink, carrying a sceptre and wearing a purple cloak.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
The Archbishop of Nova Justiniana and All Cyprus is elected with lay participation.

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: Cyprus was evangelised in the apostolic age.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Shares Greek Byzantine liturgy and theology and close ties with Constantinople.

influencedBy.name: Latin rule (1191–1571)
influencedBy.text: Under Lusignan and Venetian rule, Latin bishops subordinated the Orthodox hierarchy, a memory that shaped Cypriot identity.

influenced.name: Cypriot nationalism
influenced.text: Archbishop Makarios III led the struggle for independence and became the republic's first president in 1960.

influenced.name: Orthodox Church of Ukraine
influenced.text: Archbishop Chrysostomos II recognised the OCU in 2020, a decision that divided the Cypriot synod.

keyFigures.name: Barnabas
keyFigures.role: Apostle and native of Cyprus, venerated as founder of the church.

keyFigures.name: Epiphanius of Salamis
keyFigures.role: 4th-century bishop and anti-heretical writer.

keyFigures.name: Makarios III
keyFigures.role: Archbishop (1950–77) and first President of Cyprus.

keyFigures.name: Chrysostomos II
keyFigures.role: Archbishop from 2006 until his death in 2022.

keyFigures.name: Georgios III
keyFigures.role: Archbishop since December 2022.

denomProfiles.tagline: Minority Orthodox church of Poland's east, rooted among Belarusians, Ukrainians and Lemkos.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Received autocephaly from Constantinople in 1924, arguing that Kyiv's transfer to Moscow in 1686 had been uncanonical.
Moscow, which had rejected the 1924 grant, issued its own grant of autocephaly in 1948.
Has declined to recognise the Orthodox Church of Ukraine.
focuses: Preserving the faith of national minorities in a predominantly Catholic country.
Pilgrimage and spiritual life centred on the Holy Mountain of Grabarka.
Theological education at the Christian Theological Academy in Warsaw.
Remembrance of 20th-century suffering, including the destruction of churches in the 1930s and the deportations of 1947.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic, with growing use of Polish.
Keeps the Julian calendar.
The annual pilgrimage to Grabarka on the feast of the Transfiguration (19 August), where pilgrims leave crosses.
Led by the Metropolitan of Warsaw and All Poland; Metropolitan Sawa (Hrycuniak) has served since 1998.

influencedBy.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Most of its dioceses belonged to the Russian church before 1918.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Granted its autocephaly in 1924.

influencedBy.name: Orthodox of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
influencedBy.text: It continues the Orthodox tradition of the old Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

influenced.name: Orthodox of Czech Lands and Slovakia
influenced.text: Its bishops helped establish the hierarchy of the Orthodox Church of the Czech Lands and Slovakia after 1945.

influenced.name: Belarusian and Lemko culture in Poland
influenced.text: Parishes are centres of minority language and culture in Podlasie and elsewhere.

keyFigures.name: Dionizy (Waledyński)
keyFigures.role: Metropolitan of Warsaw who led the church to autocephaly in 1924.

keyFigures.name: Sawa (Hrycuniak)
keyFigures.role: Metropolitan of Warsaw and All Poland since 1998.

denomProfiles.tagline: Church rebuilt from near-extinction after Albania's state atheism.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Proclaimed autocephaly at the Congress of Berat (1922), recognised by Constantinople in 1937.
Stresses Albanian-language worship as part of its national and pastoral identity.
Under Anastasios developed a theology of mission, reconciliation and interfaith respect in a Muslim-majority society.
focuses: Rebuilding parishes, churches and clergy after the total ban on religion (1967–90).
Education, healthcare and social services open to all Albanians.
Peaceful coexistence with Muslims and Catholics.
Training a new generation of clergy at the Resurrection of Christ Theological Academy at Shën Vlash near Durrës.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Albanian and Greek.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
The Resurrection Cathedral in Tirana (consecrated 2014) symbolises the church's revival.
Led by the Archbishop of Tirana, Durrës and All Albania with the Holy Synod.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Albania's Orthodox had been under Constantinople; it recognised autocephaly in 1937 and sent Anastasios in 1991.

influencedBy.name: Albanian Orthodox Church in America
influencedBy.text: Fan Noli's Boston-based church (1908) pioneered the Albanian-language liturgy.

influencedBy.name: Church of Greece
influencedBy.text: Greek theological training and missionary experience shaped its post-1992 revival.

influenced.name: Orthodox mission theology
influenced.text: Anastasios's experience in Africa and Albania influenced Orthodox thinking on mission worldwide.

influenced.name: Albanian national culture
influenced.text: The vernacular liturgy contributed to the Albanian national awakening in the early 20th century.

keyFigures.name: Fan Noli
keyFigures.role: Priest, statesman and translator who led the Albanian Orthodox movement.

keyFigures.name: Kristofor Kisi
keyFigures.role: First Archbishop after recognition of autocephaly in 1937.

keyFigures.name: Anastasios (Yannoulatos)
keyFigures.role: Archbishop from 1992 until his death in 2025, who rebuilt the church.

keyFigures.name: Joan (Pelushi)
keyFigures.role: Archbishop elected in 2025.

denomProfiles.tagline: English-speaking American Orthodox church grown from the Russian mission to Alaska.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Received autocephaly from the Moscow Patriarchate in 1970; Constantinople and most other churches have not recognised it.
Holds that the Orthodox in North America should form one local, territorial church rather than ethnic jurisdictions.
Its liturgical theology, shaped by Alexander Schmemann, centres the Church on the Eucharist.
focuses: Mission to English-speaking Americans and converts.
Theological education at St Vladimir's (founded 1938) and St Tikhon's seminaries.
The goal of a unified American Orthodox church.
Liturgical renewal and frequent Communion.
practices: Byzantine liturgy mainly in English, with some Church Slavonic, Romanian, Albanian and Spanish.
Most parishes use the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
Led by a Metropolitan of All America and Canada and a Holy Synod.
Includes ethnic dioceses (Romanian, Albanian, Bulgarian) alongside territorial ones.

influencedBy.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Valaam monks reached Kodiak in 1794, and the Russian mission diocese grew into the OCA.

influencedBy.name: Carpatho-Rusyn Greek Catholics
influencedBy.text: Alexis Toth led thousands of Rusyn Greek Catholics into Orthodoxy from 1891.

influencedBy.name: Russian émigré theology
influencedBy.text: Paris-trained theologians such as Schmemann and Meyendorff brought the 'Paris school' to America.

influenced.name: American convert Orthodoxy
influenced.text: Its English-language life and seminaries attracted many American converts.

influenced.name: Liturgical theology
influenced.text: Schmemann's 'For the Life of the World' shaped Orthodox and Western liturgical thought.

keyFigures.name: Herman of Alaska
keyFigures.role: Valaam monk in Alaska; in 1970 the first saint canonised in America.

keyFigures.name: Innocent (Veniaminov)
keyFigures.role: Missionary bishop and translator in Alaska, later Metropolitan of Moscow.

keyFigures.name: Tikhon of Moscow
keyFigures.role: Archbishop in America (1898–1907) before becoming Patriarch.

keyFigures.name: Alexander Schmemann
keyFigures.role: Dean of St Vladimir's Seminary and liturgical theologian.

keyFigures.name: Alexis Toth
keyFigures.role: Former Greek Catholic priest who led many Rusyns into Orthodoxy.

denomProfiles.tagline: Ukrainian autocephalous church recognised by Constantinople in 2019.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Holds, with Constantinople, that Kyiv was never canonically transferred to Moscow and that Constantinople could grant autocephaly.
Its Tomos (January 2019) makes it autocephalous but leaves Constantinople the preparation of the holy myron and certain appeals.
Rejects the 'Russian world' ideology as incompatible with Orthodox teaching.
focuses: Ukrainian national and spiritual independence, especially since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Receiving parishes that leave the Moscow-linked Ukrainian Orthodox Church.
Ukrainian-language worship and church life.
Pastoral care of soldiers, refugees and victims of war.
practices: Byzantine liturgy in Ukrainian, with some Church Slavonic.
Moved to the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts on 1 September 2023, so Christmas falls on 25 December.
Led by the Metropolitan of Kyiv and All Ukraine; Epiphanius (Dumenko) was elected in 2018.
Recognised by Constantinople, Alexandria, Greece and Cyprus; Moscow and most other churches do not recognise it.

influencedBy.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
influencedBy.text: Convened the 2018 unification council and issued the Tomos of autocephaly.

influencedBy.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Most of its clergy and liturgical tradition come from the Russian synodal era.

influencedBy.name: Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Autocephalist movements of 1921, 1942 and 1990 preceded it and merged into it.

influencedBy.name: Petro Mohyla
influencedBy.text: The 17th-century Metropolitan of Kyiv is honoured as a model of Kyivan Orthodox learning.

influenced.name: Debate on autocephaly
influenced.text: Its creation provoked a split between Moscow and Constantinople and a wider argument over who may grant autocephaly.

keyFigures.name: Vladimir (Volodymyr) the Great
keyFigures.role: Prince of Kyiv whose baptism (988) Ukrainians claim as their own origin.

keyFigures.name: Bartholomew I
keyFigures.role: Ecumenical Patriarch who signed the Tomos in 2019.

keyFigures.name: Epiphanius (Dumenko)
keyFigures.role: Metropolitan of Kyiv and All Ukraine since 2018.

keyFigures.name: Filaret (Denysenko)
keyFigures.role: Former head of the Kyiv Patriarchate who supported union but later withdrew.

denomProfiles.tagline: Russian Orthodox who kept the pre-1650s rites after Nikon's reforms.
coreDoctrines: Hold that the pre-Nikonian rites and books, inherited from Muscovite tradition, preserve the true Orthodox faith unchanged.
Saw Nikon's reforms and the anathemas of the 1666–67 councils as apostasy; some interpreted them as signs of the end times.
Priestly groups (popovtsy) retain bishops and the Eucharist; the Belokrinitsa hierarchy dates from 1846.
Priestless groups (bezpopovtsy) hold that valid priesthood ended, and practise lay-led worship without the Eucharist.
focuses: Faithful preservation of liturgical forms, chant, icons and manuscripts.
Communal discipline and separation from 'the world'.
Memory of martyrs such as Archpriest Avvakum and Boyarina Morozova.
Economic self-reliance; Old Believer merchants and industrialists were prominent in 19th-century Russia.
practices: Sign of the cross with two fingers and a double, not triple, Alleluia.
Use of pre-reform service books, znamenny chant and the eight-pointed cross.
Baptism by full triple immersion; men often wear beards.
Communities in Russia, the Baltic states, Romania (Lipovans) and in the Americas and Australia.
Some are in communion with the Moscow Patriarchate under the Edinoverie arrangement of 1800.

influencedBy.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: They continue the Muscovite church tradition before the 1650s.

influencedBy.name: Stoglav Council (1551)
influencedBy.text: This Muscovite council endorsed practices such as the two-finger sign that the Old Believers defend.

influenced.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influenced.text: It lifted the anathemas on the old rites in 1971 and tolerates them within the Edinoverie.

influenced.name: Russian culture and art
influenced.text: Old Believer collectors preserved many icons and manuscripts and patronised Russian art.

keyFigures.name: Avvakum Petrov
keyFigures.role: Archpriest and author of an autobiographical Life, burned in 1682.

keyFigures.name: Feodosia Morozova
keyFigures.role: Noblewoman who died in prison in 1675, painted by Surikov.

keyFigures.name: Andrei Denisov
keyFigures.role: Leader of the priestless Vyg community in northern Russia.

keyFigures.name: Ambrose of Belokrinitsa
keyFigures.role: Former Metropolitan of Sarajevo whose joining in 1846 gave priestly Old Believers a hierarchy.

denomProfiles.tagline: Émigré Russian Orthodox church, self-governing within the Moscow Patriarchate since 2007.
coreDoctrines: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Originated under Patriarch Tikhon's 1920 decree allowing cut-off dioceses to govern themselves.
Rejected Metropolitan Sergius's 1927 declaration of loyalty to the Soviet state.
Canonised the New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia, including the imperial family, in 1981.
Since the 2007 Act of Canonical Communion it is a self-governing part of the Russian Orthodox Church.
focuses: Preserving Russian Orthodox tradition in emigration.
Strict liturgical and ascetic traditionalism.
Monastic life, especially Holy Trinity Monastery in Jordanville, New York.
Mission among Western converts in English and other languages.
practices: Keeps the Julian calendar.
Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic, with English, German and other languages in the diaspora.
Governed by a Synod of Bishops based in New York and led by a First Hierarch.
Venerates John Maximovitch of Shanghai and San Francisco (canonised 1994).

influencedBy.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Its bishops and tradition come from the pre-revolutionary Russian church.

influencedBy.name: White emigration
influencedBy.text: Its founders were émigré bishops gathered at Sremski Karlovci in Serbia in 1920–21.

influencedBy.name: Serbian Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: The Serbian church hosted its synod between the wars.

influenced.name: Western convert Orthodoxy
influenced.text: Writers such as Seraphim Rose drew many Western converts to traditional Orthodoxy.

influenced.name: Russian Orthodox Church
influenced.text: Its canonisation of the New Martyrs influenced the Moscow Patriarchate's own canonisation in 2000.

keyFigures.name: Anthony (Khrapovitsky)
keyFigures.role: First head of the synod abroad (1920–36).

keyFigures.name: John (Maximovitch)
keyFigures.role: Archbishop of Shanghai and San Francisco, canonised in 1994.

keyFigures.name: Seraphim Rose
keyFigures.role: American convert monk and writer of the Platina monastery.

keyFigures.name: Laurus (Škurla)
keyFigures.role: First Hierarch who signed the 2007 Act of Canonical Communion.

denomProfiles.tagline: Ancient non-Chalcedonian churches confessing one incarnate nature of God the Word.
coreDoctrines: Accept the first three Ecumenical Councils (Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Ephesus 431) and reject Chalcedon (451).
Confess Christ's single united divine-human nature, following Cyril's formula 'one incarnate nature of God the Word' (miaphysitism).
Reject both Nestorianism and the Eutychian view that Christ's humanity was absorbed into his divinity.
Joint statements with the Eastern Orthodox (1989–90) and Catholic common declarations agree that the differences are largely terminological.
Hold Holy Tradition and the Fathers as authoritative alongside Scripture.
focuses: Survival of ancient Christian communities in Egypt, Syria, Armenia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and India.
Monasticism and fasting as central disciplines.
Preservation of ancient liturgical languages: Coptic, Syriac, Classical Armenian and Ge'ez.
Ecumenical dialogue with Eastern Orthodox and Catholics.
practices: Six autocephalous churches (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Malankara) in communion but without a single head.
Ancient liturgies such as those of St Basil, St James and the Armenian Badarak.
Infants receive baptism, chrismation and Communion together.
Strict and frequent fasting, often abstaining from all animal products.

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: They see themselves as the continuation of the pre-Chalcedonian Church.

influencedBy.name: Cyril of Alexandria
influencedBy.text: His Christology is the foundation of their teaching.

influencedBy.name: Severus of Antioch
influencedBy.text: The 6th-century patriarch was the leading theologian of the anti-Chalcedonian movement.

influenced.name: Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church
influenced.text: Syriac Orthodox bishop Gregorios Abdul Jaleel's arrival in 1665 linked Indian St Thomas Christians to the Syriac Orthodox Church.

influenced.name: Eastern Catholic Churches
influenced.text: Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian Catholic churches separated from them.

influenced.name: Modern ecumenical Christology
influenced.text: Their dialogues helped clarify that Chalcedonians and non-Chalcedonians share the same faith in substance.

keyFigures.name: Cyril of Alexandria
keyFigures.role: Theologian of the one incarnate nature.

keyFigures.name: Dioscorus of Alexandria
keyFigures.role: Patriarch deposed at Chalcedon, honoured as a saint by the Copts.

keyFigures.name: Severus of Antioch
keyFigures.role: Leading 6th-century anti-Chalcedonian theologian.

keyFigures.name: Jacob Baradaeus
keyFigures.role: 6th-century bishop who ordained a separate hierarchy across Syria.

denomProfiles.inIndia: Kerala's Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and Jacobite Syrian Christian Church, heirs of the St Thomas Christians, are the main Oriental Orthodox churches in India, alongside a small Armenian presence in Kolkata and Chennai.

denomProfiles.tagline: Egypt's ancient church of St Mark, mother of monasticism.
coreDoctrines: Holds the miaphysite Christology of Cyril of Alexandria and rejects the Council of Chalcedon.
Claims apostolic foundation by Mark the Evangelist; its head is the Pope of Alexandria.
Accepts the first three Ecumenical Councils and seven sacraments.
Teaches that salvation is received through faith, the sacraments and a life of repentance and good works.
Venerates the martyrs and the Virgin Mary; Marian apparitions such as Zeitoun (1968) are widely honoured.
focuses: The monastic heritage of Antony, Pachomius and the Desert Fathers, renewed by a 20th-century monastic revival.
Sunday schools and religious education, from Habib Girgis's movement (1918).
Martyrdom and endurance amid sectarian violence in Egypt and Libya.
Care for a growing worldwide diaspora.
practices: Liturgies of St Basil, St Gregory and St Cyril in Coptic and Arabic, with cymbals and triangles.
Uses the Coptic calendar, counting years from the Era of the Martyrs (AD 284).
Very extensive fasting: over 200 days a year without animal products.
Many Copts bear a small cross tattoo on the wrist.
Pope Shenouda III (1971–2012) and Pope Tawadros II (since 2012) have led a period of expansion.

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: Alexandria was a major centre of the early Church.

influencedBy.name: Alexandrian school
influencedBy.text: Clement, Origen and the catechetical school shaped Alexandrian theology.

influencedBy.name: Desert Fathers
influencedBy.text: Egyptian monasticism started with Antony and Pachomius in the 4th century.

influenced.name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
influenced.text: Ethiopia's metropolitans were Egyptian monks sent by Alexandria until 1959.

influenced.name: Coptic Catholic Church
influenced.text: A Catholic branch separated in the 18th century.

influenced.name: Western monasticism
influenced.text: Through John Cassian and others, Egyptian monastic teaching shaped Benedictine and wider Western monastic life.

keyFigures.name: Mark the Evangelist
keyFigures.role: Traditional founder and first bishop of Alexandria.

keyFigures.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
keyFigures.role: 4th-century patriarch and defender of Nicaea.

keyFigures.name: Antony of Egypt
keyFigures.role: Father of Christian monasticism.

keyFigures.name: Cyril of Alexandria
keyFigures.role: Theologian of the Council of Ephesus.

keyFigures.name: Shenouda III
keyFigures.role: Pope (1971–2012) who expanded the church's education and diaspora.

denomProfiles.tagline: Africa's ancient Christian kingdom church, keeping Ge'ez worship and the tabot.
coreDoctrines: Tewahedo ('made one') expresses the miaphysite faith in the one united nature of Christ.
Accepts the first three Ecumenical Councils and rejects Chalcedon.
Has the broadest biblical canon in Christianity, often counted as 81 books, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees.
Keeps some Old Testament observances, such as both Sabbath and Sunday, circumcision and dietary laws, as part of its tradition.
Honours the Virgin Mary and the saints intensely, with many monthly feasts.
focuses: Worship and chant, with the zema chant ascribed to St Yared.
Monasticism and church schools that train priests and debtera (lay scholar-singers).
Ethiopian national and cultural identity.
Fasting and pilgrimage, especially to Lalibela and Aksum.
practices: Every church has a tabot, a consecrated altar tablet representing the Ark of the Covenant.
Liturgy in Ge'ez, with increasing use of Amharic and other languages.
Fasts about 180–250 days a year, depending on the person's status.
Great festivals such as Timket (Epiphany) and Meskel (the Finding of the True Cross).
Autocephalous under its own Patriarch since 1959; Abune Mathias has served since 2013.

influencedBy.name: Coptic Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Its bishops came from Egypt from the 4th century until 1959.

influencedBy.name: The Nine Saints
influencedBy.text: Syrian monks of the late 5th century spread monasticism and translated texts.

influencedBy.name: Kebra Nagast
influencedBy.text: The 14th-century 'Glory of the Kings' links the Solomonic dynasty and the Ark to Ethiopia.

influenced.name: Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church
influenced.text: Became autocephalous in 1993 after Eritrean independence.

influenced.name: Ethiopianism
influenced.text: Its antiquity inspired African Christian independence movements and later Rastafari.

influenced.name: Ethiopian Catholic Church
influenced.text: A Catholic branch of Ge'ez rite separated from it.

keyFigures.name: Frumentius
keyFigures.role: First bishop of Aksum, consecrated by Athanasius.

keyFigures.name: Ezana of Aksum
keyFigures.role: King who adopted Christianity in the 4th century.

keyFigures.name: Yared
keyFigures.role: 6th-century composer of Ethiopian sacred chant.

keyFigures.name: Zara Yaqob
keyFigures.role: 15th-century emperor and church reformer.

keyFigures.name: Abune Basilios
keyFigures.role: First Ethiopian-born Patriarch (1959).

members.note: About 43.5% of Ethiopia's population declared Orthodox in the 2007 national census; later surveys suggest a lower share.

denomProfiles.tagline: Church of the first Christian nation and of the Armenian people worldwide.
coreDoctrines: Holds the miaphysite Christology of Cyril and does not accept the Council of Chalcedon, a position settled at councils of Dvin from 506.
Claims apostolic foundation by Thaddeus and Bartholomew, and national conversion under Gregory the Illuminator.
Accepts the first three Ecumenical Councils and seven sacraments.
Canonised the victims of the 1915 Armenian Genocide as martyrs in 2015.
focuses: Preservation of Armenian identity, language and culture, especially in the diaspora.
Remembrance of the genocide and survival of Armenian communities.
Patristic and literary heritage, from Mesrop Mashtots to Gregory of Narek.
Ecumenical relations with Catholics and other Orthodox.
practices: The Badarak (Divine Liturgy) in Classical Armenian, using unleavened bread and unmixed wine.
Celebrates Christmas and Theophany together on 6 January.
Mother See at Holy Etchmiadzin, led by the Catholicos of All Armenians, with a second Catholicosate of Cilicia in Antelias, Lebanon.
Patriarchates in Jerusalem and Constantinople; the madagh (blessed sacrificial meal) and carved khachkar crosses.
Married priests and celibate vardapets (doctors of the church), from whom bishops are chosen.

influencedBy.name: The Early Church
influencedBy.text: Christianity reached Armenia early and became the royal faith under Tiridates III.

influencedBy.name: Syriac Christianity
influencedBy.text: Early Armenian liturgy and literature drew on Syriac and Greek traditions.

influencedBy.name: Battle of Avarayr (451)
influencedBy.text: The defence of Christianity against Persian Zoroastrianism became a defining national memory.

influenced.name: Armenian Catholicosate of Cilicia
influenced.text: The Cilician see continued as a separate catholicosate after 1441.

influenced.name: Armenian Catholic Church
influenced.text: A Catholic branch formed in 1742.

influenced.name: Armenian literature
influenced.text: The alphabet invented by Mesrop Mashtots for Bible translation founded Armenian letters.

keyFigures.name: Gregory the Illuminator
keyFigures.role: Evangelist of Armenia and first Catholicos.

keyFigures.name: Mesrop Mashtots
keyFigures.role: Inventor of the Armenian alphabet.

keyFigures.name: Gregory of Narek
keyFigures.role: 10th-century mystic poet, declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope Francis in 2015.

keyFigures.name: Nerses Shnorhali
keyFigures.role: 12th-century Catholicos, hymn-writer and ecumenist.

keyFigures.name: Karekin II
keyFigures.role: Catholicos of All Armenians since 1999.

denomProfiles.inIndia: A small but historic Armenian community has churches in Kolkata (Holy Nazareth, built 1724) and Chennai (St Mary's, 1772), and the Armenian College and Philanthropic Academy in Kolkata (1821).
